title: Counting the Quiet Hours
bodyMd:
**Social science.** This passage is adapted from an original essay on the measurement of unpaid work. The table that follows the passage reports results from the diary study the passage describes.

For most of the twentieth century, national statistical agencies measured what a country produced and largely ignored what it maintained. Meals cooked, children supervised, elderly relatives visited: none of it entered the accounts, because none of it was paid. The gap was not a secret. It was a matter of method — a survey that asks “What is your occupation?” cannot see work that has no job title.

Time-use diaries were supposed to close the gap, and to a degree they did. A diary asks respondents to record what they were doing in each interval of a day, usually ten or fifteen minutes long, and a coder then assigns each entry to a category. Applied across a representative sample, the method produces an estimate of how a whole population spends its hours, whether or not anyone was paid for them.

But diaries inherited a problem from the surveys they replaced. Early coding schemes allowed only one activity per interval, which forced respondents and coders alike to choose. A parent folding laundry while supervising a toddler recorded laundry, because laundry is the thing with a name. The sociologist Devika Raut has argued that this single-activity rule did not merely undercount care in general; it systematically undercounted the kind of care that consists of being available — supervision, vigilance, the readiness to intervene — precisely because such care rarely displaces another task.

Raut’s remedy was a second column. In the diaries her team fielded in three regions, respondents recorded a primary activity and, optionally, anything they were simultaneously responsible for. The secondary column roughly doubled recorded childcare time in every region. Critics note that the second column also invites overstatement, since a respondent may claim responsibility for a sleeping child in a distant room. Raut’s reply is that the direction of the earlier error was known and the direction of the new one is not, and that a measure which is uncertain is an improvement on one that was reliably wrong.

data.caption: Mean hours of childcare recorded per adult per week in Raut’s three-region diary study, under the single-activity rule and with the secondary column added.

accessibilityText: A four-paragraph social science passage about how unpaid care work is measured, followed by a table of three rows. The passage explains that occupation surveys could not see unpaid work, that time-use diaries were introduced to close the gap, that early diaries allowed only one activity per interval and so hid care that consists of being available, and that the sociologist Devika Raut added an optional second column for simultaneous responsibility, which critics say invites overstatement. The table gives mean childcare hours per adult per week for three regions under two coding rules. Northern: 11.2 hours with the primary column only, and 21.9 hours with the primary plus secondary columns. Coastal: 13.5 hours primary only, and 26.4 hours primary plus secondary. Interior: 9.8 hours primary only, and 20.6 hours primary plus secondary. All names, regions and figures are invented.

provenance.notes: Original social science passage and invented data set written for this bank. Devika Raut, the three regions and every figure in the table are fictional; nothing here is drawn from, or modelled on, any published ACT Reading passage or any real study.
